prediction_ref.short_label: Herdr publishes a paid tier above its Apache-2.0 runtime by Q2 2027

validation_rows.evidence_summary: Herdr said on Thursday, August 6 that it has joined Y Combinator's F26 batch and, in the same post, relicensed its runtime from AGPL to Apache-2.0. Herdr is a terminal runtime for command-line coding agents: it organises them into panes, tabs and projects and keeps them running persistently on a single machine, with separate machines left disconnected from each other. No funding figure appears in the announcement, and a batch admission is not a round, so nothing here attaches a number to the company. prediction_ref.short_label: Terminal coding agents refuse commands the operator approved by H1 2027

validation_rows.evidence_summary: Alex Wauters published an analysis on the Scale X blog on Wednesday, August 5 of an interactive browser game in which the player stands in for the human approver of a coding agent, accepting or denying each command under time pressure. Across more than 40,000 runs and roughly 409,000 approve-or-deny decisions, mean accuracy was 66.3%. The shape matters more than the mean: miss rates ran 11.7% on obviously destructive commands, 23.8% on persistent mutation attacks, 33.4% on exfiltration and code execution, and 35.0% on scope violations, so the further a hostile command sits from the thing people are trained to fear, the more reliably it gets waved through. 35.2% of players caught every threat but only 20.8% did so while blocking no more than one in five safe commands; 7% approved everything, and 32.9% of sessions ended on a negative score. The most-missed single command was npm run analyze, approved 64.7% of the time even though the malicious payload was visible in the history log rather than in the prompt the player was asked to judge. The author is explicit that the setting is artificial - threats appeared in 34% of commands, far above any real workload - and his own conclusion is to put the check in the tool layer, where the payload is inspected, rather than in the approval prompt, where only the command line is. Two other items describe the layer this pushes into. Meta published Muse Code on Wednesday, August 5, a terminal coding agent explicitly in beta whose subagents are asynchronous, persist for the whole session and decide themselves when to report back, with every approval appended to a local event log; approvals plainly still exist there, and the pace at which command lines arrive in front of one person is set by a scheduler. Herdr, describing its terminal runtime on Thursday, August 6, keeps agents running persistently on the machine they sit on. And the cost objection to a payload-reading check moved on Tuesday, August 4, when Liquid AI published LFM2.5-2.6B, a 2.6-billion-parameter model for planning, tool calls and multi-step tasks that fits under 2.5 GB of memory, on the company's own unreproduced figures. Nothing published today describes any harness refusing a command its operator approved.

validation_rows.evidence_summary: [REVIVED] Meta's Muse Code, published on Wednesday, August 5 and explicitly labelled beta, brings the two ingredients together in one harness without joining them into the primitive this prediction names. Approvals exist and are recorded: every model call, tool run, approval and edit is appended to a local event log. Durability exists: Meta describes that log as making the agent replay-exact and restart-safe, so after a crash it resumes precisely where it stopped rather than re-deriving state from the working tree. What the announcement does not describe is a suspend-and-resume checkpoint - an agent pausing mid-run on a question, persisting that pending state, and continuing from the answer rather than re-prompting the model. The subagent design pushes against that shape: the subagents are asynchronous, persist for the whole session rather than being spawned per task, and decide themselves when to report back, which is a model built to avoid waiting on anyone. The Scale X analysis published on Wednesday, August 5 supplies the reason the pause matters anyway, at 66.3% mean accuracy across roughly 409,000 approve-or-deny decisions made under time pressure.
